PSSP-MFFNet: A Multifeature Fusion Network for Protein Secondary
Structure Prediction
Yifu Chen,# Guanxing Chen,# and Calvin Yu-Chian Chen*
Cite This: ACS Omega 2024, 9, 5985−5994
Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
Article Recommendations
ABSTRACT: Protein secondary structure prediction (PSSP) is a fundamental task in
modern bioinformatics research and is particularly important for uncovering the
functional mechanisms of proteins. To improve the accuracy of PSSP, various general
and essential features generated from amino acid sequences are often used for
predicting the secondary structure. In this paper, we propose PSSP-MFFNet, a deep
learning-based multi-feature fusion network for PSSP, which incorporates a multi-view
deep learning architecture with the multiple sequence alignment (MSA) Transformer
to efficiently capture global and local features of protein sequences. In practice, PSSP-
MFFNet adopts a multi-feature fusion strategy, integrating different features generated
from protein sequences, including MSA, sequence information, evolutionary
information, and hidden state information. Moreover, we employ the MSA
Transformer to interleave row and column attention across the input MSA. A hybrid
network architecture of convolutional neural networks and long short-term memory
networks is applied to extract high-level features after feature fusion. Furthermore, we introduce a transformer encoder to enhance
the extracted high-level features. Comparative experimental results on independent tests demonstrate that PSSP-MFFNet has
excellent generalization ability, outperforming other state-of-the-art PSSP models by an average of 1% on public benchmarks,
including CASP12, CASP13, CASP14, TEST2018, and CB513. Our method can contribute to a better understanding of the
biological functions of proteins, which has significant implications for drug discovery, disease diagnosis, and protein engineering.
■INTRODUCTION
Proteins are essential compounds for all living organisms to
carry out life activities. The function of a protein depends on
its structure, making the study of protein sequence, structure,
and spatial folding of extraordinary significance for under-
standing its biological function.1 Understanding protein
function and interactions between different proteins relies on
knowledge of the specific structure of proteins, making
research on protein structure particularly urgent. Currently,
X-ray crystallography and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)
are the mainstream experimental methods used to probe the
structure of proteins.2 However, these methods for determin-
ing the structure have disadvantages such as high cost and
extended time requirements. Therefore, more advanced
machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) methods
have been widely used in protein structure prediction, leading
to significant progress.3,4
With the development of sequencing technology and related
research, the number of protein primary structure sequences
(i.e., amino acid sequence of protein composition) has
exponentially increased, and many of these sequences have
been stored in large biological databases. However, due to the
complex arrangement and diverse structures of amino acids
under the tertiary structure, it is extremely challenging to
directly use the primary structure to the predict tertiary
structure. Further research often requires the help of secondary
structure prediction results. Protein secondary structure, which
describes the local spatial structure of a protein, acts as an
intermediary connecting primary and tertiary structures,
making it helpful for predicting protein tertiary structure.5
Therefore, improving the accuracy of protein secondary
structure prediction (PSSP) is a critical task in structural
biology.
The lack of accurate protein secondary structure, which
relies heavily on sequence information, limits the prediction of
protein tertiary structures and functions. Therefore, integrating
extra secondary structure information is expected to improve
the accuracy of prediction. AlphaFold26 demonstrates
remarkable accuracy in predicting protein structures solely
from their amino acid sequences. The key factor contributing
to the success of AlphaFold2 lies in its precise extraction of
coevolutionary information from multiple sequence alignments

(MSAs). Leveraging coevolutionary information for contact
prediction and structure modeling has been an extensively
explored concept. However, previous attempts have fallen
short of desired outcomes due to insufficiently strong or
excessively noisy coevolutionary signals present within the
MSAs. Rao et al.7 proposed the MSA transformer model, an
unsupervised protein language model using the MSA of a
query sequence instead of a single query sequence. The model
uses row and column attention of input MSAs and masked
language modeling objectives. With the help of the attention
algorithm, a truly accurate extraction of actual residue signals

from MSAs becomes available. Therefore, it is significant to
introduce MSA features into the PSSP task to improve the
prediction accuracy of the model. In this paper, we propose
PSSP-MFFNet, whose flowchart is illustrated in Figure 1.
PSSP-MFFNet is a DL-based PSSP multi-feature fusion
network that combines a multiview deep learning architecture
and MSA Transformer to efficiently capture global and local
features of protein sequences.
The main contributions and advantages of this article are as
follows:
• We present PSSP-MFFNet for PSSP, which integrates
four types of feature representation approaches to
explore different sequential information.
• We introduce an MSA Transformer to interleave row
and column attention across the input MSA and apply a
hybrid network architecture of CNN and LSTM
networks to extract high-latent features after feature
fusion.
• Extensive comparative experiments on benchmark data
sets demonstrate that PSSP-MFFNet significantly out-
performs state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods on inde-
pendent tests. It outperforms other models by 1% on
average on public benchmarks, including CASP12,
CASP13, CASP14, TEST2018, and CB513.
■RELATED WORK
Protein Secondary Structure Prediction. PSSP aims to
classify each amino acid on a protein sequence and express
local structure with secondary structure tags. The secondary
structure (SS) involves hydrogen bonding along the main
chain, resulting in the folding of long chains into local shapes
that are primarily α helix (H), beta-strand (E), and coil (C).8
Early prediction methods mainly used amino acid residues to
perform propensity statistics of specific fragments and later
developed more complex statistical models. However, the
effects were poor and could not meet actual needs.9
In recent years, researchers have proposed various DL-based
methods to predict the protein secondary structure. SPOT-
1D10 combines a variety of DL models, mainly using a
combination of bidirectional recurrent neural networks and
long short-term memory (LSTM) networks and adding a
residual convolutional neural network (CNN). It considers not
only local features between amino acids but also captures more
distant amino acid information, resulting in a significant
improvement in prediction accuracy.
DeepCNF11 adopts a combination of deep CNN and
conditional random field to obtain the global optimal solution
by considering the relationship between amino acid residues
and labels. It achieves 84.4 and 84.7% Q3 accuracy on CASP10
and CASP11 data sets, respectively. MUFOLD-SS12 is based
on the Deep3I network and consists of two nested initial
modules, a convolutional layer, and a fully connected (FC)
layer. It can perform convolution operations to efficiently
handle local and global interactions between amino acid
residues, further improving the prediction accuracy. Senior et
al. use a neural network model to compare gaps between
amino acid residues, which can predict more structural
information and achieve higher accuracy for fewer homologous
sequences.13 Hu et al. proposed an ensemble model based on a
bidirectional LSTM neural network. The ensemble model
consists of five parts, each with different input features. Each
subsection has a loss function, and their output is combined to
obtain the final classification result.14
MSA Transformer. MSA is a sequence alignment of
multiple homologous protein sequences of the target protein.15
Rao et al.7 proposed the MSA Transformer model, an
unsupervised protein language model that uses the MSA of
query sequences instead of a single query sequence. Experi-
ments show that the model accurately predicts long-range
contacts between residues. The model uses row and column
attention and a masked language modeling objective. More-
over, the model accurately predicted other properties of the
protein, such as secondary structure prediction and mutational
effects. These results demonstrate that the MSA Transformer
model can efficiently extract protein sequence features from
the MSA profiles.
Position-Specific Scoring Matrix. Although the number
of proteins with unknown structures and functions is rapidly
increasing, it is possible that proteins with unknown structures
and proteins with known structures come from the same or
similar gene families.16 Therefore, the similarity of protein
sequences has become an important starting point for
researchers to study protein structure and function. From
this perspective, there is still a lot of useful information to be
extracted by comparing protein sequences of unknown
structure with known protein sequences. The PSI-BLAST
tool17 is often used to compare the similarity of protein
sequences in databases to obtain the resulting PSSM profile.
The commonly used research method is to construct a PSSM
as the input of the classifier. The proposal of PSSM has
effectively improved the classification accuracy of 3-state

Hidden Markov Model. A hidden Markov model (HMM)
is a dynamic statistical model that can be described by a finite-
state machine.22 HMMs are particularly suitable for processing
one-dimensional sequences. They can be trained to obtain
probabilistic transition matrices for each state, thus describing
different protein families. In PSSP, HMMs learn structures
such as α helix (H), beta-strand (E), and coil (C) and apply
these HMMs to new protein sequences with unknown
secondary structures. The HMMER 3.3.2 tool23 is commonly
used to generate HMM profiles from protein sequences.
■RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
In this paper, we propose PSSP-MFFNet, a novel deep
learning-based multi-feature fusion network for PSSP. Figure 2
illustrates the architecture of the proposed PSSP-MFFNet. The
method consists of four main modules: (1) the multi-feature
fusion module, (2) the feature extraction module, (3) the
feature enhancement module, and (4) the prediction module.
We use the MSA Transformer,7 which is a pre-trained model
learned from 26 million MSAs, to extract features from MSA
profiles generated from protein sequences. In the multi-feature
fusion module, we integrate four feature metrics, including
MSA feature, PSSM feature, HMM feature, and sequence
embedding feature, using a cosine similarity-based fusion
strategy.24 For feature extraction and enhancement, we use a
hybrid neural network of CNN and LSTM to obtain local and
global features from fused features. A Transformer encoder25 is
applied to process intermediate features before passing them to
the prediction module. Finally, the generated features are fed
into the prediction module to predict the secondary structure
corresponding to each position.
Data Set. To make a fair comparison with the most recent
state-of-the-art methods, we train and validate the PSSP-
MFFNet framework on the training set and validation set of
CullPDB.26 We use CB513,27 CASP12, CASP13, CASP14,28
and TEST201829 to evaluate the performance of our method
and conduct comparisons with previous methods. The data
sets mentioned above are displayed in Table 1.
For the CullPDB data set, 6133 proteins were extracted from
the CullPDB server with resolution <2.5 Å, R-factor <1.0 and
sequence identity< 25% between any protein pair according to
BlastClust.17 After redundancy filtering with CB513, the
CullPDB data set is divided into 5600 training samples, 256
validation samples, and 272 testing samples. In this work, we
only use training and validation sets from the CullPDB data
set. CB51327 is a classic and widely used benchmark data set.
After excluding the sequence similarity between CULLPDB
and CB153, we take CB513 as one of our testing sets.

Comparison Experiment. We compare our method with
previous SOTA methods for PSSP on several data sets. Table 2
shows the experimental results on the CB513 data set. Our
model achieves SOTA with an ACC of 0.8613. PSSP-MFFNet
shows the superiority of the SOTA method on ACC metrics,
obtaining an improvement of 1% compared with the SOTA
method. The results show that our multi-feature fusion and
hybrid neural network can effectively improve the accuracy of
PSSP. The evaluation results on the CASP data sets and
TEST2018 show the same superior performance in Tables 3
and 4. PSSP-MFFNet achieved the highest performance on the
CASP12, CASP13, and CASP14 data sets, with ACC of
0.8218, 0.8014, and 0.8191, respectively. In TEST2018, PSSP-
MFFNet took first place with an ACC of 0.8696. Overall, the
results on CASPs and TEST2018 are about 1% better than the
SOTA methods on ACC.
Due to its authority in the field of protein structure
prediction, AlphaFold’s performance is considered an industry
standard. By comparison with AlphaFold, we can validate the
performance of our model and evaluate its accuracy, thus
increasing the confidence and reliability of our research work.
By performing mean pooling and Max pooling on the
penultimate layer of the AlphaFold network, we added an
additional 1D output head to the network for predicting
secondary structure labels. In CASP14, the accuracy of Q3
prediction by the AlphaFold network is 83%, which is about
1% higher than the prediction accuracy of our model. It is
worth noting that AlphaFold requires 128 TPUs to train over
11 days to complete. However, our model needs to be trained
on only one NVIDIA GeForce RTX A6000 GPU for 10 days
to obtain the results in the experiment. During training, our
model required only 25% of the memory size of AlphaFold. In
future work, we will continue to improve the prediction
accuracy based on the model’s lightweight and inference speed.

Additionally, we conduct another ablation experiment to
investigate the necessity and validity of different components
of PSSP-MFFNet. The results of the ablation experiments
performed on the CB513 data set are shown in Table 6. Since
we have designed multiple components in the decoder, we
tested the performance of the models for lacking CNN layers,
lacking LSTM layers, or lacking Feature Enhancement. The
experimental results demonstrate that the prediction accuracy
of PSSP-MFFNet decreases to varying degrees in the absence
of any component, with the most significant decrease in
accuracy occurring when the CNN layers are removed. Thus,
we can conclude that the complete PSSP-MFFNet demon-
strates optimal performance and all components we have
designed are essential for its functionality.
Visualization of Performance Comparison. To intui-
tively compare the performance of PSSP-MFFNet and existing
methods, we use PyMOL30 to map the secondary structure to
the tertiary structure. We randomly selected two proteins with
Protein Data Bank identities and compared different methods
for predicting their secondary structures. As illustrated in
Figure 3, we test the performance of PSSP-MFFNet, OPUS-
TASS, and MUFold-SS on two proteins (PDB ID: 1HZ6 and
2JYO). The red area represents α helix (H), the purple area
represents beta-strand (E) and the green area represents coil
(C). The visualization results demonstrate that the predictions
of PSSP-MFFNet are closer to the ground truth than those of
other methods. Based on this, we can conclude that PSSP-
MFFNet has better performance than existing methods.
Case Study. To verify the accuracy of our model’s
predictions at mutation sites, we conduct experiments using
SARS-CoV-2 proteins and apply our PSSP-MFFNet for
secondary structure prediction. COVID-19 is a highly
infectious respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2
virus. The virus has four structural proteins - spike (S),
envelope (E), membrane (M), and nucleocapsid (N)
proteins.31 The spike protein consists of two subunits, S1
and S2, and plays a critical role in interacting with host cell
receptors, making it a primary target for designing COVID-19
vaccines.
Mutations in the receptor binding domain (RBD) of the
SARS-CoV-2 spike protein have given rise to new variants of
concern, such as the Delta and the Omicron strains. Therefore,
we select the SPIKE_7N9T protein and several representative
proteins from the new variants to perform structure prediction.
As illustrated in Figure 4, we show the homology of the
selected protein in the Phylogenetic Tree and present the
predicted structures of our method. The red area represents
incorrect predictions, while the green area represents correct
predictions. Additionally, we make the nonmutation sites
transparent to highlight the prediction results at the mutation
sites. The experimental results demonstrate an accuracy rate of
94.51% in the mutation area and an overall prediction
accuracy rate of 96.35%. These findings suggest that PSSP-
MFFNet performs well at the mutation sites.

■CONCLUSIONS AND OUTLOOK
In this study, we developed PSSP-MFFNet, a DL-based multi-
feature fusion network for PSSP, which achieved superior
performance in predicting secondary structures of proteins. By
combining multiple feature representations, such as MSA,
PSSM, HMM, and sequence embedding, our multi-feature
fusion strategy effectively enhanced the feature representation,
leading to improved prediction accuracy. The novel hybrid
network architecture of PSSP-MFFNet, consisting of a CNN
and LSTM, extracted both local and global features of protein
sequences, which contributed to the high accuracy of our
model. Through ablation studies, we demonstrated that each
component of PSSP-MFFNet played a critical role in achieving
a high accuracy, validating the effectiveness of our method.
Importantly, PSSP-MFFNet outperformed existing methods
on several data sets, which is a significant breakthrough in the
field of PSSP.
Furthermore, PSSP-MFFNet has the potential to integrate
additional structural information on proteins, providing a more
efficient way to explore protein structures and leading to a
better understanding of their biological functions. Our study
has implications for various areas of research, including drug
discovery, disease diagnosis, and protein engineering. The
ability of our method to integrate multiple feature
representations and extract both global and local features can
enhance our understanding of protein structures and functions.
Compared to other PSSP models, PSSP-MFFNet has better
performance, and the prediction results are closer to the
ground truth.
In conclusion, PSSP-MFFNet not only offers a new
approach for PSSP but also provides a potential for integrating
additional structural information of proteins. Our method can
contribute to a better understanding of the biological functions
of proteins, which has significant implications for drug
discovery, disease diagnosis, and protein engineering. PSSP-
MFFNet is an encouraging method that can significantly
improve prediction accuracy, provide new research insights,
and facilitate the development of new therapeutics and
diagnostic tools in the field of protein structure prediction.
■METHODOLOGY
Multi-feature Fusion. In this section, we describe how we

preprocess protein sequences to generate different feature
representations that can be used in machine learning
algorithms for training. We introduce four different types of
features: MSA feature, PSSM feature, HMM feature, and
sequence embedding feature, and we explain how we apply an
embedding method to obtain each type of feature. To generate
a unified feature space, we also introduce a Cosine-Similarity-
based feature fusion strategy.24
MSA Feature Generation. For a given protein sequence, we
use HHblits ver. 3.3.0 together with the uniclust30_2018_0832
database to generate the MSA profiles of target sequences.
Then, we extract evolutionary information with the MSA
Transformer. We define the input MSA as a character matrix r
× c, where r and c are rows (number of sequences) and
columns (sequence length) in the MSA, respectively. After
encoding by the MSA Transformer, the input MSA is
embedded into two kinds of features: (1) One is an r × c ×
768 tensor. Then, as the neuron size decreases, the dimension
of this feature is reduced to 128 through three linear layers.
After horizontal and vertical expansion and stacking, this
feature is to form a query sequence feature of a c × c × 256
tensor, represented as Fseq. (2) The other one is row attention
maps, represented as Attent.
The MSA Transformer has a 12-stacked 12-head encoder.
So, there are a total of 144 attention maps stacked in the shape
of c × c × 144. The extracted row attention map and input
features are then concatenated in the feature dimension to a
2D feature map, which is a c × c × 400 tensor, called MSA
feature. Then, the feature dimension of the MSA feature is
reduced to 64 through three 2D convolutional layers, each of
which is followed by an instance normalization and a Rectified
Linear Unit(ReLU) activation. We use symbol FMSA to
represent the generated MSA feature, the MSA Transformer

PSSM Feature Generation. In this paper, we generate the
PSSM profile for each given protein sequence using four
iterations of the position-specific iterative basic local alignment
search tool (PSI-BLAST)17 with the Uniprot_sprot database33
with default parameters. The resulting PSSM is represented as
a c × n matrix, where c is the length of the protein sequence
and n is the number of standard amino acid residues. The
PSSM score represents the position-specific score of the 20
amino acids at a specific position in the sequence, and the
score is typically a positive or negative integer. Therefore, we
can use the PSSM score to determine the likelihood that an
amino acid at a given position has evolved toward another
amino acid with a higher score, thus potentially indicating a
more stable structure.
HMM Feature Generation. The HHM profiles we use in
this study are generated using HMMER 3.3.223 with default
parameters and a default sequence database. We also define the
generated HHM profile as a c × n matrix, where c is the length
of each protein sequence and n is the number of standard
residues. HHM matrix scores are usually displayed as positive
nonintegers. As a stochastic model, the HMM is widely used to
predict protein secondary structure. In this study, the explicit
sequence is the protein sequence, and the hidden state is their
secondary structure. An HMM can be trained to obtain
probabilistic transition matrices for each state, thereby
describing different protein families. In PSSP, HMMs are
used to learn α helix (H), beta-strand (E), and coil (C)
structures and applied to new protein sequences with unknown
secondary structures.
Sequence Embedding Feature Generation. Here, we apply
word2vec34 to generate sequential features from protein
sequences. We define the input protein sequences as the r ×
c matrix, where r is the batch size and c is the length of each
protein sequence. The output of word2vec is an r × c ×
embedding_dim, where embedding_dim represents the dimen-
sion of the embedding vector, that is, how many dimensions
are used to represent a symbol. Here, we set the
embedding_dim = 20. Applying the Word2vec model, our
method can learn high-quality residual vectors with latent
semantics and prevent zero-redundant representations.

Hybrid Neural Network. The hybrid neural network in
PSSP-MFFNet is composed of a CNN and an LSTM. To
extract features, the hybrid neural network takes the high-latent
features as input. The CNN is used to extract local features,
while LSTM aims to extract global features. The fused features
generated by the previous module are first input into a CNN
consisting of a 2D convolutional layer, a batch normalization
layer, a maximum pooling layer, and a ReLU activation
function layer. CNN is used to extract local information in the
protein feature representation since each convolution neuron
processes only the data of its receptive field. To improve

■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
Implementation Details. We employ PyTorch36 to build
the model. The MSA Transformer used in the multi-feature
fusion module is a pre-trained version. We adopted batch
normalization and dropout techniques to speed up the training
of the network and improve its performance. We insert a

employ batch normalization (1) in the CNN, (2) between the
LSTMs, and (3) between the feature extraction module and
the feature enhancement module. By adding the network layer
of controlling the mean and variance, batch normalization can
reduce internal covariate shifts. In the MSE restriction,
parameter λ is set to 0.1, while balance coefficient γ is set to
0.1 in the total loss. Considering the different number of
residues in three structural states, we define a weighted
secondary structure label in the formula to calculate Loss3 in
Ltotal, which means the weight of state E is 1.25, while H and C
are 1. During the training phase, we fix the parameters in the
MSA Transformer. Other parameters of PSSP-MFFNet are
trained by the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 × 10−3.
The entire model was trained on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX
A6000 GPU for about 100 epochs and took about 10 days.
